video_title: Worry List Is Growing More Worrisome
gist: Ed Yardeni's Monday morning client call argues that a Middle East escalation — Iran's IRGC proxies, with the Houthis advancing on control of the Red Sea strait — has pushed oil above $100 toward $110, driven the 10-year Treasury yield back to 5%, and boxed in both Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent; he expects a 25bp rate HIKE at the coming FOMC and possibly a hiking cycle. He keeps his year-end S&P 500 target at 8,400 (now $425 of earnings times a 19.7 multiple) because forward earnings and revenues keep making record highs, but raises his subjective odds of a bearish/recessionary outcome from 20% to 30%, calls energy the obvious overweight hedge, and expects a pullback or roughly 10% correction rather than a bear market.

themes.theme: Fed Turns to Hiking Under Warsh

insights.claim: Ed Yardeni expects Fed Chair Kevin Warsh to deliver a 25 basis point rate HIKE at the upcoming FOMC meeting and to signal at the press conference that this may not be one-and-done but the start of a hiking cycle of another one or two increases.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A hiking Fed inverts the consensus easing trade — front-end duration, rate-sensitive equities and carry strategies are all positioned the wrong way if this is right.
insights.quote: I think Borsch will deliver a 25% uh rate hike um at the FOMC meeting. I think he will at the press conference uh remain hawkish about inflation

insights.claim: The two-year Treasury yield is currently signaling three rate hikes over the next 12 to 24 months, which would fully reverse the prior year's 75 basis points of cuts.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: The front end already prices a full reversal of the easing cycle — a market-implied benchmark for judging whether the Fed is behind or ahead of the curve.
insights.quote: now the two-year is signaling three rate hikes uh over let's say the next 12 to 24 months which would reverse the rate cuts that we had uh last year

insights.claim: Warsh lost credibility with markets by giving hawkish June and July press conferences without acting on them, which pushed the two-year yield to price tightening on its own in a classic bond vigilante move.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: When a central bank's rhetoric and action diverge, the market prices the tightening itself — watch the 2-year rather than Fed speak for the effective policy stance.
insights.quote: if he was going to talk like a hawk then he had to walk like a hawk or at least fly like a hawk

insights.claim: Warsh's no-forward-guidance, let-the-markets-tell-us approach has become a trap because markets are now loudly demanding that the Fed get ahead of the inflation problem and raise rates.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: If policy is market-reactive by design, market pricing becomes self-fulfilling — rate expectations, not Fed communication, are the variable to track.
insights.quote: the markets are screaming at the Fed and have been screaming of late that uh they should get ahead of the inflation problem and raise rates

insights.claim: A surprise 50 basis point Fed hike would likely push the 10-year Treasury yield DOWN rather than up, because bond vigilantes want proof the Fed is being vigilant about inflation.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A counterintuitive long-duration setup: the most aggressive hike would be the bullish outcome for long bonds, inverting the naive rates-up-yields-up trade.
insights.quote: I think if they did 50 base points I think the bond yield would actually come down. Uh I think that's what the bond vigilantes the bond vigilantes want to see

themes.theme: Oil Shock as the Critical Variable

insights.claim: Houthi advances toward controlling the strait in and out of the Red Sea have driven oil above $100 and toward $110, with Goldman Sachs analysts talking about $120 oil.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A concrete price path plus a named sell-side target gives a reference band for energy equity and inflation-breakeven positioning.
insights.quote: the folks over at Goldman Sachs have I think a few last week talked about $120 oil and we're certainly over 100 and uh approaching 110

insights.claim: Yardeni identifies the price of oil as the single critical variable driving the entire macro complex right now, because higher-for-longer oil seeps into the inflation numbers and puts the Fed in a box.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Makes crude the master variable for rates and equities — Middle East de-escalation is the fastest path to relief across every asset in the chain.
insights.quote: Now, of course, um driving all this is the price of oil. That's that's really the the critical variable here here.

insights.claim: The earlier oil selloff during Middle East de-escalation revealed how much physical oil actually exists in the world, implying the current spike is a geopolitical risk premium that can unwind as fast as it appeared.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Frames the oil move as premium rather than scarcity — argues against chasing crude and for treating energy as a hedge, not a secular long.
insights.quote: when the war simmerred down and uh deescalated and there was some diplomacy going on uh we saw how much oil there really was in the world and the price of oil came tumbling down

themes.theme: Bond Yields at 5% and Treasury's Bazooka

insights.claim: Yardeni's framework puts the normal range for the 10-year Treasury yield at 4% to 5%, with the current 5% level at the very top of that range and likely to move higher unless policymakers respond.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: An explicit level framework: 5% is the range top, so duration buyers need a policy catalyst rather than mean reversion alone.
insights.quote: we still think that the normal range for the 10-year bond yield is four to 5%. But clearly we're at the top of that range right now.

insights.claim: Elevated interest rates at current levels are a healthy sign that the US economy is doing very well, contradicting President Trump's view that a best-in-the-world economy deserves the lowest rates.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Reframes rising yields as a growth signal that supports earnings even while pressuring multiples — the opposite of a stagflation read.
insights.quote: interest rates around current levels in many ways are a healthy sign. They're a sign that the US economy is very doing very very well

insights.claim: Yardeni thinks Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has to consider pulling out the bazooka — shifting debt issuance toward the bill market instead of the bond market, the same 2023 maneuver by Janet Yellen that Bessent himself had opposed.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A concrete, watchable catalyst: a refunding shift toward bills would be the signal to cover long-bond shorts.
insights.quote: I think Bessant u has to consider pulling out the bazooka.

insights.claim: The unwinding yen carry trade may be the main explanation for rising bond yields worldwide, because Japanese rate hikes and a stronger yen remove the near-zero-cost funding that financed foreign bond purchases in places like Brazil and the United States.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Identifies a global flow driver independent of US fundamentals — Japanese policy and the yen become leading indicators for global term premia.
insights.quote: that may be a good reason good explanation uh maybe the main explanation for why bond yields around the world have been been going up

insights.claim: Bessent's intervention on behalf of the yen was really intended to stop Japanese selling of US Treasuries to support their currency, and Yardeni says it unnerved markets rather than calming them.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Shows official FX action is really about defending the Treasury bid — a failed intervention signals escalating stress in foreign demand for US debt.

themes.theme: Worry List and Rising Recession Odds

insights.claim: Yardeni Research raised its subjective probability of a bearish outcome from 20% to 30% and cut its Roaring 2020s base case from 80% to 70%, treating that bearish probability as effectively its odds of a recession in the foreseeable future.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A quantified, trackable gauge from a prominent bull — a further move to 40% or 50% is his own stated trigger for lowering the index target.
insights.quote: we went from 20% to 30% as the uh the risk that it that things will not go well for the base case. And so the base case goes from 80% to 70%. That's my way of communicating that guess what I'm worried.

insights.claim: The best real-time recession warning indicators to watch are weekly initial unemployment claims and weekly Redbook same-store retail sales on the consumer side, plus company guidance in the coming earnings season on the capital spending side.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A concrete weekly-frequency dashboard for front-running official data on recession risk.

insights.claim: Small-cap relative performance is a useful gauge of the market's perception of recession risk because small caps are especially sensitive to recession fears.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Small-cap versus large-cap relative strength becomes a live market-implied recession probability alongside the macro data.
insights.quote: Small caps tend to be especially sensitive to fears of of a recession.

insights.claim: Yardeni still expects no recession, noting his Roaring 2020s thesis has survived what he calls the most widely anticipated recession of all time with three years of the decade left to run.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Anchors the constructive case: absent a recession, analyst estimates historically hold and equities grind higher through the noise.
insights.quote: we've had the most widely anticipated recession of all times that just didn't happen uh so far

insights.claim: Yardeni Research is keeping its S&P 500 year-end target at 8,400 while raising its year-end earnings estimate from $415 to $425 per share, which lowers the required multiple from 20.2 to 19.7.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: The explicit EPS-times-multiple arithmetic behind a street target lets investors stress-test it directly against their own multiple assumptions.
insights.quote: 425 * 19.7 multiple uh gives us 8,400

insights.claim: Consensus 2027 S&P 500 earnings expectations have risen to a record $419.54, up from $415 only a few weeks earlier, and Yardeni now considers $425 realistic by year-end.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Rising rather than falling forward estimates is the load-bearing support for equities in a rising-rate environment; a stall here breaks the bull case.
insights.quote: we're at $41,9.54 on the 20 27 number. That's uh pretty impressive.

insights.claim: This bull market is unusual because analysts keep raising earnings expectations rather than cutting them into earnings season, a pattern Yardeni labels FEMO — fabulous earnings momentum.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Inverts the usual playbook where stocks rise despite estimate cuts — a reversion to downward revisions would be the regime change to watch.
insights.quote: It's been FIMO fabulous earnings momentum

insights.claim: The mark-to-market capital gains flattering S&P 500 forward earnings come from only two or three companies and sit in the 2026 number, while forward earnings are converging toward 2027 estimates that exclude mark-to-market forecasts.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Means the underlying earnings strength is cleaner than headline forward EPS implies — a rebuttal to the claim that index earnings are inflated by non-operating gains.

insights.claim: Analysts' long-term growth expectations have hit an all-time record of 26.7% annual earnings growth over the next 3 to 5 years, which Yardeni calls impossible and explicitly labels irrational exuberance even though it is grounded in genuinely strong recent earnings.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A named sentiment extreme flagged by a bull — record bottom-up long-term growth expectations are a classic late-cycle warning even while near-term estimates hold.
insights.quote: there's no way that earnings are going to grow 26.7% on an annual basis over the next 3 to 5 years

insights.claim: S&P 500 forward revenues continue to make new highs despite the Russia-Ukraine war, the Middle East situation, higher oil and rising yields, and Yardeni treats forward revenues as a proxy for global rather than merely US revenues.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Turns S&P forward revenues into a usable real-time global growth indicator whose continued strength contradicts the geopolitical-slowdown narrative.

insights.claim: Yardeni's mechanism for this bull market is that forward earnings rise faster than the forward P/E falls, so the index advances even while the multiple compresses.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Reframes de-rating as compatible with rising prices, which changes how investors should read multiple compression in a rising-rate regime.
insights.quote: forward earnings continues to uh go up. Uh the forward PE continues to go down. Uh and uh the market goes up uh because on balance forward earnings go up faster than the the PE goes down.

themes.theme: AI Regulation and the Capex Paradox

insights.claim: Yardeni frames the sudden AI-doom narrative as originating from the AI industry itself, which would not mind being regulated, raising the prospect of regulatory capture in which the industry guides the regulators.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: If incumbents shape AI rules, regulation becomes a moat rather than a cost — favoring large incumbents over challengers and open-source competitors.
insights.quote: whether the AI industry wants the government to regulate them and then the AI industry will capture the regulators and kind of guide things the way they want them to go

insights.claim: A specific goal of the US AI industry in seeking regulation is to put limits or restraints on the open-source models coming out of China, even as President Trump argues the US should not regulate AI because the Chinese will race ahead.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Identifies Chinese open-source models as the competitive threat driving US AI policy — a direct read on pricing power for closed-model vendors.

insights.claim: Yardeni argues the market no longer knows what it is rooting for on AI, since a slowdown in AI capital spending would stop depleting free cash flow and could help corporate profits even as it undercuts the growth narrative.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Names the two-sided AI trade: a capex slowdown is bearish for suppliers but bullish for hyperscaler cash flow, so the sign of the equity impact depends where you sit in the chain.
insights.quote: if that suddenly slows, shouldn't that be a positive? Uh wouldn't that be a good good thing for corporate cash flow or maybe even uh corporate profits?

insights.claim: Yardeni agrees that if AI spending slows, bond yields could fall because of less crowding out, which would in turn boost the equity multiple.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Supplies a partial offset for the index: an AI capex disappointment could be cushioned by lower rates and multiple expansion.
insights.quote: If AI spending slows, could bond yields drop as there is less of a crowding out effect and that could boost the multiple? The answer is sure.

insights.claim: Yardeni Research has been overweight energy for a while, the S&P 500 energy sector is outperforming as oil rises, and Yardeni calls energy the obvious overweight to hold as a hedge against the current geopolitical and inflation developments.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: An explicit, currently-working sector hedge tied directly to the Red Sea oil risk.
insights.quote: we think uh energy is probably the is the obvious uh overweight position to have as a hedge against all these uh developments of late

insights.claim: With the S&P 500 not far off its all-time high, Yardeni expects a pullback that could become roughly a 10% correction but not a bear market unless the current pressures produce a recession, and he views such a correction as creating buying opportunities.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Sets both a magnitude and a rule: buy the 10% drawdown unless recession evidence actually shows up in claims and company guidance.
insights.quote: I don't think this is going to be a bare market. Uh this could be a a 10% correction. Uh I suppose u but I think it will create buying opportunities

insights.claim: Yardeni expects bull-bear sentiment ratios to turn sharply bearish over the next couple of weeks, consistent with September's history as a tough month that sometimes spills into October.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A contrarian sentiment washout in a seasonally weak window is exactly the setup his buy-the-correction rule is designed to exploit.
insights.quote: I would not be surprised to see the bull bear ratios turning very bearish very coming down sharply over the next couple of weeks

insights.claim: If the correction deepens, Yardeni expects a total market takedown rather than a rotation out of tech into value, healthcare and staples, despite the broadening earlier in the year when the equal-weight S&P 500 and small caps were outperforming.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Warns that defensive rotation will not protect capital in this drawdown — correlations converge, so cash or hedges beat sector rotation.
insights.quote: I I think it probably more of a total takedown than rotation.

insights.claim: Yardeni sees no immediate relief for the bond market from fundamentals because neither a sudden weakening in the economy nor a sudden drop in inflation is in the cards, leaving the outcome dependent on whether Bessent and Warsh produce a coordinated policy response.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Makes policy coordination, not incoming data, the binary catalyst for bonds — position around the FOMC and Treasury announcements rather than macro prints.
insights.quote: doesn't look to me as though that there's any uh immediate relief coming from the from the fundamentals
